title: Why Koreans Ask Your Blood Type on a First Date
description:
In Korea and Japan, your blood type isn't just medical info — it's your personality profile. Type A? Organized but anxious. Type B? Creative but selfish. It's on dating profiles, job applications, and first-date conversations.

But the origin of this belief is genuinely dark. Like, wartime-racial-classification dark. And the psychological trick keeping it alive is the same one behind every horoscope you've ever read.

The twist? The pseudoscience actually CREATES the personality differences it claims to measure.

What's your blood type? Does the personality match? Comment below!

sections.narration: Imagine this. You're on a first date in Seoul. Coffee shop. Good vibes. The conversation flows. Then your date leans forward, makes direct eye contact, and asks — completely seriously — what's your blood type? Not your zodiac sign. Not your MBTI. Your literal blood type. The stuff on your medical records. And based on your answer — two letters — they will decide whether you're worth a second date. If that sounds insane, welcome to South Korea and Japan, where blood type personality theory is as culturally embedded as astrology is in the West. Except people take it significantly more seriously. It's on dating app profiles. It's in job interviews. And if you're Type B? You're already at a disadvantage. But here's what nobody tells you — the origin of this belief isn't quirky pop culture. It's wartime racial classification. And the psychological trick keeping it alive will make you question every personality system you've ever believed in.
sections.visual_notes: Scene 1: Ji-woo at a cute Seoul cafe — Min-ho across from her, leaning forward intensely. Scene 2: Speech bubble from Min-ho: 'What's your blood type?' — Ji-woo's confused/amused face. Scene 3: Korean dating app profile showing blood type displayed prominently. Scene 4: Four blood type labels (A, B, O, AB) like trading cards — Type B with a red warning stamp.

sections.narration: Here's how deep this goes. Each blood type has a fixed personality profile. Type A — careful, organized, anxious, perfectionist. Type O — confident, social, natural leader, stubborn. Type AB — creative, eccentric, unpredictable, hard to read. And then there's Type B. Type B is the villain of blood type theory. Selfish. Irresponsible. Unreliable. Bad at commitment. In Korean dating culture, Type B men are considered the worst romantic partners. Some people — otherwise rational, educated adults — will refuse to date a Type B. There's even a term for the discrimination. In Japan, it's called bura-hara — blood type harassment — and it's a documented social problem. People have been rejected from jobs. Children bullied in school. In a 2012 survey, over 70 percent of Japanese people said they genuinely believe blood type affects personality. This isn't fringe. It's infrastructure. But here's the question nobody asks — who started this? Who decided that two letters on a blood test determine your entire personality? The answer is uncomfortable. Really uncomfortable.
sections.visual_notes: Scene 1: Four characters for each type — Type A adjusting glasses nervously, Type O standing tall, Type AB looking quirky, Type B with red 'X' stamp. Scene 2: Ji-woo swiping left on dating app — profile says 'Type B' — auto-reject. Min-ho nodding approvingly. Scene 3: Japanese office — manager circling 'Blood Type: B' on a resume. Scene 4: Bar chart: '70% believe' — Ji-woo staring at the stat.

sections.narration: In 1927, a Japanese professor named Takeji Furukawa published a paper called The Study of Temperament Through Blood Type. Sounds academic. But his actual goal was racial classification. Imperial Japan was looking for scientific-sounding explanations for why certain ethnic groups — particularly Taiwanese and Ainu indigenous people — were supposedly inferior. Blood type distribution varies by ethnicity. Furukawa used this data to argue that personality and capability were biologically determined by blood. It was pseudoscience in service of imperialism. The theory was criticized. Furukawa lost credibility. It was mostly forgotten. Then in 1970, a journalist named Masahiko Nomi dusted it off, stripped out the racism, repackaged it as pop psychology, and wrote a bestselling book. Seven million copies. His son continued the series. TV shows picked it up. Blood type horoscopes appeared in magazines. Within a decade, what started as a tool of racial hierarchy became a fun personality quiz. Nobody remembered the origin. They just remembered the quiz. But here's the part that should bother you most — if the science is racist pseudoscience, why does it feel so accurate? The answer is a psychological trick, and you've fallen for it too.
sections.visual_notes: Scene 1: 1927 — Professor Furukawa at his desk, dark study, writing. Scene 2: Imperial Japan maps with ethnic classifications — dark, uncomfortable panel. Scene 3: 1970s transition — journalist Nomi holding colorful bestseller, crowds buying. Scene 4: Modern bookstore — blood type book shelves, TV screen with horoscope — Ji-woo picking one up.

sections.narration: Multiple large-scale studies — including one with over ten thousand participants — found zero correlation between blood type and personality. Zero. Blood type is determined by antigens on your red blood cells. A has A antigens. B has B. O has neither. AB has both. This affects transfusions. It has nothing to do with whether you're punctual or bad at relationships. So why does it feel true? The Barnum effect — the same trick behind fortune cookies and horoscopes. The descriptions are vague enough that anyone sees themselves in them. Type A is careful and anxious. Who isn't sometimes? The profiles are unfalsifiable. You always find evidence if you're looking. And when an entire culture is looking, they find it everywhere. Try this — read any horoscope and think that's SO me. Now read a different sign's. Also you. That's the Barnum effect running at national scale. But the twist goes darker than a psychological trick.
sections.visual_notes: Scene 1: Scientific paper — red stamp: 'NO CORRELATION.' Scene 2: Red blood cells with A, B, O antigens — simple diagram. Scene 3: The Barnum effect — one vague description, four people all nodding 'that's me!' Scene 4: Ji-woo reading one blood type description, nodding — reading a DIFFERENT type — nodding the same way. Realization face.

sections.narration: This belief exists almost exclusively in Japan and Korea. The rest of the world doesn't care about blood type beyond medical emergencies. But every culture has picked something arbitrary and built a personality system around it. In the West — astrology. Your birth month determines your traits. In China — your birth year animal. In India — your nakshatra, your birth star, gets checked before marriage alliances are formed. In the Middle East — coffee cup readings. In Myanmar — your day of birth determines your personality planet. Every civilization has looked at something uncontrollable — your birth date, your stars, your blood — and said this explains who you are. Korea just happened to pick the one that sounds the most scientific. Which ironically makes it the hardest to question. Because when someone says your personality is determined by antigens on your red blood cells, it sounds like biology. It sounds provable. It sounds like fact. And that's exactly why the next part is so dangerous.
sections.visual_notes: Scene 1: World map — Japan and Korea as 'BLOOD TYPE ZONE,' West as 'ZODIAC ZONE,' China as 'ANIMAL ZONE,' India as 'STAR ZONE.' Scene 2: Four panels — blood drop, zodiac wheel, Chinese zodiac animals, Indian chart. Scene 3: All four merging into one question mark — 'same idea, different wrapper.' Scene 4: Ji-woo with arms crossed — 'everyone does this, huh?' — but looking concerned, not amused.

sections.narration: Here's the twist nobody talks about — and it should concern you. Blood type personality theory, despite being completely baseless in biology, actually creates real personality differences. Through stereotype threat. If you grow up in Korea being told your entire life that Type B people are selfish — and you are Type B — research shows you may actually begin behaving more selfishly. Not because of your antigens. Because of the expectation. You internalize the label. You start performing it. Korean Type B men who are repeatedly told they're bad partners have measurably lower confidence in relationships than Type B men from countries where nobody cares about blood type. The pseudoscience became real. Not through biology — through sociology. The prophecy doesn't predict behavior. It creates it. The belief system that started as racist pseudoscience, got repackaged as entertainment, is now actively shaping the personalities of millions of people who think they're just reading a fun quiz. That should make everyone uncomfortable.
sections.visual_notes: Scene 1: Cycle diagram — 'told you're selfish' → 'believe it' → 'act selfishly' → 'see? you ARE selfish' → loop. Scene 2: Type B character starting tall and confident, shrinking frame by frame as labels pile on. Scene 3: Same character in a country where nobody cares — confident, normal, happy. Scene 4: Ji-woo and Min-ho both looking troubled — 'the belief creates the reality.'

sections.narration: Does your blood type define your personality? Biologically — not even slightly. The science is settled. But culturally, in Korea and Japan, blood type theory has become a self-reinforcing system. It started as racist pseudoscience, got repackaged as entertainment, and embedded itself so deeply that it now shapes real behavior through real discrimination. As a conversation starter? Mostly harmless. As a system that rejects people from jobs and relationships because of something on their medical chart? That's bura-hara. And it's real. Know where it came from. Use it as a quirk if you want. But don't let two letters on a blood test define who you are, who you love, or what you're capable of. That part — the only part that actually matters — has absolutely nothing to do with your blood.
sections.visual_notes: Scene 1: Ji-woo back at the cafe — Min-ho asks 'so, your blood type?' — Ji-woo smiles: 'does it matter?' Scene 2: All four blood type characters standing as equals — no hierarchy. Scene 3: Professor Furukawa's 1927 paper being filed away in a dark drawer. Scene 4: Ji-woo and Min-ho walking out of the cafe together — tagline: 'Your grandma's rules, finally explained.'
